questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The SI unit of solid angle is:

solution.concept: Supplementary units: radian and steradian
solution.explanation: In the SI system the plane angle is measured in radian (rad) and the solid angle in steradian (sr). A solid angle is the ratio of the intercepted area on a sphere to the square of its radius, so like the plane angle it is dimensionless but has a named unit.
solution.why_others_wrong: The radian and the degree are units of plane angle, not solid angle. The candela is the SI base unit of luminous intensity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', the international system of units (radian and steradian)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Repeated measurements of the period of a pendulum give a mean value of 2.50 s and a mean absolute error of 0.05 s. The percentage error in the measured period is:

solution.concept: Relative and percentage error
solution.explanation: The relative error is the mean absolute error divided by the mean value; multiplying by 100 gives the percentage error.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.02% forgets to multiply by 100 correctly (it treats 0.02 itself as a percentage); 5% writes the absolute error 0.05 as 5%; 0.2% misplaces the decimal point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', errors in measurement (relative and percentage error)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The force F needed to keep a body moving uniformly in a circle is assumed to depend only on its mass m, its speed v and the radius r of the circle, as F ∝ mˣ vʸ rᶻ. By the method of dimensions, the values of x, y and z are respectively:

solution.concept: Deducing a relation by the method of dimensions
solution.explanation: Equate the powers of M, L and T on the two sides. With m = [M], v = [L T⁻¹] and r = [L], the force [M L T⁻²] requires x = 1, y = 2 and z = −1, i.e. F ∝ mv²/r (the dimensionless constant, here 1, cannot be found this way).
solution.why_others_wrong: (1, 1, −1) gives [M T⁻¹], not a force; (1, 2, 1) gives [M L³ T⁻²]; (1, −2, 1) gives [M L⁻¹ T²].
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', deducing relations among physical quantities

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (its dimensional formula).

List-I:
A. Moment of inertia
B. Angular momentum
C. Torque
D. Power

List-II:
I. [M L² T⁻²]
II. [M L² T⁻³]
III. [M L² T⁰]
IV. [M L² T⁻¹]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dimensional formulae of rotational quantities
solution.explanation: All four quantities contain M L²; they differ only in the power of time. Moment of inertia is mr² → [M L²]; angular momentum is mvr → [M L² T⁻¹]; torque is force × distance → [M L² T⁻²]; power is force × velocity → [M L² T⁻³].
solution.shortcut: Each time derivative adds one T⁻¹: I → L (= Iω) → τ (= dL/dt); power = τω adds one more T⁻¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap neighbouring powers of T: angular momentum with torque, moment of inertia with angular momentum, or torque with power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional formulae
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a measured value is written in scientific notation, a × 10ᵇ, the power of ten does not affect the number of significant figures.
Statement II: According to the rules given in NCERT, a length written as 12300 cm (without a decimal point) has five significant figures.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Rules for counting significant figures
solution.explanation: In scientific notation all the significant digits appear in a; the factor 10ᵇ only fixes the order of magnitude, so Statement I is true. NCERT states that trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are not significant: 123 m = 12300 cm = 123000 mm has three significant figures, so Statement II is false.
steps: Statement I: 10ᵇ is irrelevant to significant figures → true
Statement II: 12300 (no decimal point) → trailing zeros not significant → 3 significant figures → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II would be true only if the number were written 12300. (with a decimal point) or as 1.2300 × 10⁴.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', significant figures
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The speed v of waves on the surface of deep water is assumed to depend only on the acceleration due to gravity g, the wavelength λ of the waves and the density ρ of the liquid. Using the method of dimensions, if the wavelength is made 4 times and the water is replaced by a liquid of twice the density, the wave speed becomes:

solution.concept: Method of dimensions: a variable whose exponent comes out zero
solution.explanation: Writing v ∝ gˣ λʸ ρᶻ and equating the powers of M, L and T gives z = 0: density is the only quantity with mass in it, so it cannot appear. Then x = y = 1/2, so v ∝ √(gλ), independent of the density.
steps: v'/v = √4 = 2 (the change of density has no effect)
solution.shortcut: A quantity is the only one containing a base dimension (here ρ with M) → its exponent must be zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: √2 times wrongly keeps ρ^(−1/2), giving √4/√2; 4 times forgets the square root; 2√2 times takes v ∝ √(gλρ).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional analysis and its applications

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The length and breadth of a rectangular plate are measured as l = (12.5 ± 0.1) cm and b = (4.2 ± 0.1) cm. The perimeter of the plate with its maximum absolute error, and the corresponding percentage error (to one decimal place), are:

solution.concept: Combination of errors in a sum
solution.explanation: For a sum the absolute errors add. The perimeter is P = 2(l + b), so ΔP = 2(Δl + Δb). The percentage error is then ΔP/P × 100; relative errors are added only for products and quotients, not for sums.
solution.why_others_wrong: (33.4 ± 0.2) cm forgets the factor 2 in P = 2(l + b); 3.2% adds the relative errors of l and b as if P were a product; (33.4 ± 0.8) cm counts the error of each of the four sides twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors (error of a sum)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car moving along a straight road with uniform acceleration increases its speed from 10 m/s to 20 m/s while covering a distance of 75 m. Its acceleration is:

solution.concept: Equation of motion v² = u² + 2as
solution.explanation: When the distance, not the time, is given, use the third equation of uniformly accelerated motion, v² = u² + 2as.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 m/s² forgets the 2 in 2as; 0.13 m/s² divides the change in speed by the distance (10/75); 3.3 m/s² adds the squares of the speeds instead of subtracting them (500/150).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 units and 5 units are inclined to each other at 30°. The magnitude of their vector (cross) product is:

solution.concept: Magnitude of the vector product
solution.explanation: |A × B| = AB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√3 uses cos 30° (the scalar product); 20 takes sin θ = 1; 9 simply adds the magnitudes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane' and 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', vector product

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball can be thrown from level ground with a speed of 30 m/s in any direction. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the greatest horizontal distance it can be thrown along the ground is:

solution.concept: Maximum horizontal range
solution.explanation: The range R = u² sin 2θ / g is greatest when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°, so R_max = u²/g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 m is u²/(2g), the greatest height for a vertical throw; 180 m is 2u²/g; 45√2 m uses sin θ = sin 45° in place of sin 2θ = sin 90°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion (horizontal range)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A vector A is multiplied by the real number −2. The resulting vector:

options.text: Has magnitude 2|A| and points along A
Has magnitude |A|/2 and points opposite to A
Has magnitude 2|A| and points opposite to A

solution.concept: Multiplication of a vector by a real number
solution.explanation: Multiplying a vector by a real number λ gives a vector of magnitude |λ| times the original. If λ is negative, the direction is reversed.
solution.why_others_wrong: A negative multiplier reverses the direction, so 'along A' is wrong; the magnitude is multiplied by 2, not divided; and a vector multiplied by a scalar is still a vector.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', multiplication of vectors by real numbers
solution.final_answer: Option D: Has magnitude 2|A| and points opposite to A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle starts from the origin at t = 0 and moves along the x-axis with velocity v = 6t − 3t², where v is in m/s and t in seconds. Its position at the instant (after t = 0) when it comes momentarily to rest is:

solution.concept: Position from velocity by integration
solution.explanation: Set v = 0 to find the instant of rest, then integrate the velocity from t = 0 to get the position, using x = 0 at t = 0.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 m keeps only the 3t² term; 2 m gives the time, not the position; 6 m multiplies the greatest speed (3 m/s, at t = 1 s) by the whole 2 s, as if the speed were constant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', instantaneous velocity and kinematic relations

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A projectile launched from level ground has a speed of 10 m/s at the highest point of its path and a time of flight of 2√3 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its angle of projection above the horizontal is:

solution.concept: Horizontal and vertical components of a projectile's velocity
solution.explanation: At the highest point only the horizontal component u cos θ remains, so u cos θ = 10 m/s. The time of flight T = 2u sin θ / g gives the vertical component u sin θ = gT/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° swaps the two components; 45° assumes the components are equal; tan⁻¹(2√3) uses u sin θ = gT, forgetting that the rise takes only half the flight time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: At the same instant, ball P is thrown vertically upward from the ground with a speed of 20 m/s, and ball Q is released from rest at a height of 40 m vertically above P's starting point. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the two balls meet after:

solution.concept: Relative motion of two bodies with the same acceleration
solution.explanation: Both balls have the same acceleration g, so the acceleration of one relative to the other is zero. Relative to Q, ball P moves upward at a constant 20 m/s, and it must close a gap of 40 m.
solution.shortcut: Same acceleration → treat the gap as closing at the constant relative speed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 s is P's time of flight; 2√2 s is the time Q alone would take to fall 40 m; 1 s halves the correct time by adding the two speeds wrongly (40/40).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', relative velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The position x of a particle moving along the x-axis is given by each relation in List-I (x in metres, t in seconds, t ≥ 0). Match List-I with the description of the motion in List-II.

List-I:
A. x = 5
B. x = 3t
C. x = 2t²
D. x = 4t − t²

List-II:
I. Constant acceleration opposite to the initial velocity; the particle stops at t = 2 s and then moves back
II. Constant non-zero velocity, zero acceleration
III. At rest
IV. Starts from rest with constant acceleration along +x

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Reading velocity and acceleration from x(t)
solution.explanation: Differentiate each relation once for the velocity and twice for the acceleration.
steps: x = 3t: v = 3 m/s, a = 0 → uniform velocity (II)
x = 2t²: v = 4t (0 at t = 0), a = 4 m/s² → from rest with constant acceleration (IV)
x = 4t − t²: v = 4 − 2t, a = −2 m/s² → stops at t = 2 s and returns (I)
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes confuse a constant position (rest) with a constant velocity, or exchange the two accelerated motions, which differ in the sign of the acceleration relative to the initial velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', position-time graphs and kinematic relations
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A particle moving in a plane with a constant acceleration must always move along a parabolic path.
Statement II: For a particle moving in a plane with a constant acceleration a, its position vector at time t is r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at², where r₀ and v₀ are its position and velocity at t = 0.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration
solution.explanation: The vector relation r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at² holds for any constant acceleration, so Statement II is true. The path is a parabola only when v₀ is not parallel to a; if v₀ is zero or parallel (or antiparallel) to a, the particle moves along a straight line. So Statement I is false.
steps: Statement II: integrate a = constant twice → r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at² → true
Statement I: v₀ ∥ a (e.g. a ball thrown straight up) → straight-line path → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I ignores the special case of initial velocity along the acceleration, such as vertical throws under gravity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', motion in a plane with constant acceleration
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground. Its velocity is directed at 45° above the horizontal at t = 1 s and at 45° below the horizontal at t = 3 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the angle of projection above the horizontal is:

solution.concept: Components of projectile velocity at two instants
solution.explanation: The horizontal component u_x is constant and the vertical component falls as u_y − gt. At 45° above, u_y − g(1) = u_x; at 45° below, u_y − g(3) = −u_x. Solving gives both components.
steps: Adding: 2u_y = 40 → u_y = 20 m/s, so u_x = 10 m/s
solution.shortcut: By symmetry the highest point is midway, at t = 2 s, so u_y = 2g = 20 m/s; then u_x = u_y − g(1).
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° assumes the launch direction equals the direction at t = 1 s; tan⁻¹(1/2) inverts the ratio of components; 60° would need u_y/u_x = √3.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The two diagonals of a parallelogram are represented by the vectors P = 3î + ĵ − 2k̂ and Q = î − 3ĵ + 4k̂. The area of the parallelogram is:

solution.concept: Area of a parallelogram from its diagonals
solution.explanation: If the sides are a and b, the diagonals are P = a + b and Q = a − b (or b − a). Then P × Q = −2(a × b) in magnitude 2|a × b|, so the area |a × b| equals ½|P × Q|.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√3 uses |P × Q| directly, as if P and Q were the sides; 20√3 doubles instead of halving; (5√3)/2 halves twice, mixing up the area of a triangle with that of the parallelogram.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', vector product of two vectors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If two non-parallel vectors A and B have equal magnitudes, the vectors (A + B) and (A − B) are perpendicular to each other.
Reason (R): (A + B) · (A − B) = A² − B², where A and B are the magnitudes of the two vectors.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Scalar product and perpendicularity
solution.explanation: Expanding the scalar product, (A + B)·(A − B) = A·A − A·B + B·A − B·B = A² − B², because the scalar product is commutative. When A = B this is zero, and a zero scalar product of two non-zero vectors means they are perpendicular. So R is exactly the reason for A.
steps: A = B → product = 0 → (A + B) ⊥ (A − B) (A true)
R directly gives A → option A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate fact: setting A = B in R is the whole proof of A, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the scalar product
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with a speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) It rises to a maximum height of 20 m.
(b) At t = 3 s, it is 15 m above the ground.
(c) The distance it travels in the first 3 s is 25 m.
(d) At t = 3 s, its velocity is 10 m/s directed upward.
(e) Its average velocity over the first 4 s is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Vertical motion under gravity: displacement versus distance
solution.explanation: The ball rises for u/g = 2 s to a height u²/2g = 20 m and is back on the ground at 2u/g = 4 s. After 2 s it falls, so its velocity at 3 s is downward.
steps: (c) 20 m up in 2 s, then 5 m down in the next 1 s → 25 m, true
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) has the right speed but the wrong direction: after the highest point (t = 2 s) the ball moves down. Every option without (c) or including (d) is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block placed on a plank begins to slide down when one end of the plank is slowly raised until the plank makes an angle of 37° with the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). The coefficient of static friction between the block and the plank is:

solution.concept: Angle of repose
solution.explanation: At the angle of repose θᵣ the component of weight along the incline just equals the limiting static friction: mg sin θᵣ = μₛ mg cos θᵣ, so μₛ = tan θᵣ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.6 is sin 37° and 0.8 is cos 37°, not their ratio; 1.33 is cot 37°, the ratio taken upside down.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction (angle of repose)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text: A car of mass 1000 kg takes a turn of radius 50 m on a level (unbanked) road at a steady speed of 10 m/s. The magnitude of the frictional force exerted by the road on the car is:

solution.concept: Friction as the centripetal force on a level road
solution.explanation: On a level road the only horizontal force on the car is static friction, so it alone supplies the centripetal force mv²/r. It need not be the limiting value μₛN.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 N uses mv/r (speed not squared); 20000 N uses mv²/r with r = 5 m; 10000 N is the weight mg, which would be μN with μ = 1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', circular motion (car on a level road)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block is released from rest on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its speed after it has slid 10 m along the incline is:

solution.concept: Motion on a smooth inclined plane
solution.explanation: On a smooth incline the only force along the plane is the component of weight mg sin θ, so the block accelerates uniformly at g sin θ along the incline.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√3 m/s uses g cos θ as the acceleration; 10√2 m/s uses the full g (free fall through 10 m); 5 m/s gives the acceleration value instead of the speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a contact force?

options.text: The frictional force between a block and the floor
The gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon
The normal reaction of a table on a book
The tension in a string pulling a block

solution.concept: Contact and non-contact forces
solution.explanation: Friction, the normal reaction and the tension in a string act only when bodies touch. Gravitational (and magnetic) forces act across a distance, without contact.
steps: Friction, normal force, tension → contact forces
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three forces all need physical contact between the bodies concerned.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', introduction (contact and non-contact forces)
solution.final_answer: Option B: The gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three blocks of masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg lie in a line on a smooth horizontal table, in that order, joined by two light horizontal strings (1 kg to 2 kg, and 2 kg to 3 kg). A horizontal force of 12 N pulls the 3 kg block away from the others. The tension in the string joining the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks is:

solution.concept: Connected bodies: tension from the free-body diagram of the trailing part
solution.explanation: All three blocks have the same acceleration. The string between the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks pulls the 1 kg and 2 kg blocks together, so its tension equals their combined mass times the acceleration.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 N is the tension in the other string (1 kg × 2 m/s²); 10 N subtracts only the 1 kg block's share from 12 N; 4 N uses the 2 kg block alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law and the dynamics of connected bodies

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block slides onto a rough horizontal floor with a speed of 10 m/s. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², the distance it slides before coming to rest is:

solution.concept: Retardation due to kinetic friction
solution.explanation: The only horizontal force is kinetic friction μₖmg, so the retardation is μₖg, independent of the mass.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 m forgets the 2 in u²/(2a); 5 m is the value of the retardation; 2 m is the stopping time (u/a = 2 s) written as a distance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction (kinetic friction)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On a smooth horizontal surface, a ball of mass 2 kg moving due east at 3 m/s collides with a ball of mass 1 kg moving due north at 6 m/s. The balls stick together. The speed of the combined body just after the collision is:

solution.concept: Conservation of momentum in two dimensions
solution.explanation: With no external horizontal force, the total momentum is conserved as a vector. Conserve each component separately and combine.
steps: East: 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s; North: 1 × 6 = 6 kg m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 m/s adds the two momenta as scalars (12/3); 6√2 m/s is the magnitude of the total momentum, not divided by the total mass; 2 m/s is only one component of the final velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A body of mass 2 kg moves as described in List-I (SI units). Match List-I with List-II (magnitude of the net force on the body).

List-I:
A. It moves with a constant velocity v = (3î + 4ĵ) m/s
B. Its position along a straight line is x = 2t²
C. It moves uniformly on a circle of radius 2 m with a speed of 3 m/s
D. Its linear momentum along a straight line is p = 6t

List-II:
I. 9 N
II. Zero
III. 6 N
IV. 8 N

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Net force from the state of motion
solution.explanation: Newton's second law: F = dp/dt = ma. Constant velocity means zero net force; in uniform circular motion the net force is mv²/r.
steps: B: a = d²x/dt² = 4 m/s² → F = 8 N (IV)
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes give x = 2t² the value 6 N (taking a = 2t² differentiated once) or swap the circular-motion and momentum cases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Newton's second law is a local relation: the force at a point at a certain instant determines the acceleration at that point at that instant, independent of the history of motion.
Statement II: A stone is dropped from the window of a train that is accelerating along a level track. Just after its release, the stone has the train's horizontal acceleration in addition to the acceleration g (neglect air resistance).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Second law as a local relation
solution.explanation: Statement I is NCERT's description of the second law. For the stone: once it leaves the hand, no horizontal force acts on it (air resistance neglected), so by this local relation its acceleration is g, vertically downward, at once. It keeps the train's horizontal velocity at the instant of release, but not the train's acceleration. So Statement II is false.
steps: Statement I: acceleration depends only on the force at that instant → true
Statement II: after release, horizontal force = 0 → horizontal acceleration = 0 → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses velocity, which the stone keeps, with acceleration, which depends only on the force acting at that instant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three concurrent forces of magnitudes 7 N, 8 N and 13 N keep a particle in equilibrium. The angle between the directions of the 7 N and the 8 N forces is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium of three concurrent forces
solution.explanation: In equilibrium the 13 N force is equal and opposite to the resultant of the other two, so the resultant of the 7 N and 8 N forces has magnitude 13 N. Use R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120° is the interior angle of the triangle of forces (180° − 60°), not the angle between the force directions; 90° assumes the forces form a right angle; 30° results from using sin θ for cos θ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block takes twice as long to slide from rest down a rough plane inclined at 45° as it would take to slide the same distance from rest down a smooth plane of the same inclination. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the rough plane is:

solution.concept: Motion on a rough incline compared with a smooth one
solution.explanation: From rest, s = ½at², so for the same distance t ∝ 1/√a. Twice the time means one quarter of the acceleration. On the rough plane a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ); on the smooth plane a = g sin θ.
steps: sin θ − μ cos θ = (sin θ)/4
solution.shortcut: μ = tan θ (1 − 1/n²) when the time is n times as long.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 takes t ∝ 1/a (forgetting the square root); 0.25 writes μ = tan θ/n²; 1.33 inverts the ratio 3/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction on an inclined plane

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a car turns sharply to the left, a passenger sitting on the right side is pressed against the right-hand door.
Reason (R): The passenger's body tends to keep moving in a straight line because of inertia, so the car turns towards the left under the passenger until the door pushes on the passenger and supplies the centripetal force needed to turn.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Inertia of direction and the centripetal force
solution.explanation: Seen from the ground, no force pushes the passenger outward. Her body tends to continue in its original straight line (first law); the car turns left beneath her, so the right-hand door moves into her, and the door's push towards the centre of the turn supplies the centripetal force. This is exactly why she is pressed against the door.
steps: R: true, it is the first-law explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the explanation, not a separate fact, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong. The common wrong idea is an outward 'centrifugal' force, which R correctly avoids.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's first law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Blocks of masses 2 kg and 3 kg are placed in contact on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction between each block and the floor is 0.2. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to the 2 kg block, pushing both blocks along together. Take g = 10 m/s². Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The acceleration of the blocks is 2 m/s².
(b) The 2 kg block pushes the 3 kg block with a force of 12 N.
(c) If the same 20 N force were instead applied to the 3 kg block, pushing the blocks the other way, the contact force between them would be 8 N.
(d) The net force on the 2 kg block is 8 N.
(e) The friction force on the 3 kg block is 10 N.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Connected bodies with friction: free-body diagrams
solution.explanation: Total friction = 0.2 × 50 = 10 N, so the common acceleration is (20 − 10)/5 = 2 m/s². The contact force on the leading block must accelerate it and overcome its own friction.
steps: (d) net force on 2 kg = 2 × 2 = 4 N, not 8 N → false
(e) friction on 3 kg = 0.2 × 30 = 6 N; 10 N is the total friction on both → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) confuses the net force with the contact force on the other block; (e) uses the total friction on both blocks for one of them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction and the dynamics of connected bodies

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 2 kg moves with a velocity v = (3î + 4ĵ) m/s. Its kinetic energy is:

solution.concept: Kinetic energy from a velocity vector
solution.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, v² = v·v = vₓ² + v_y². It is a scalar.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49 J squares the sum of the components, (3 + 4)²; 50 J forgets the ½; 5 J is the speed in m/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', kinetic energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 2 kg is dropped from rest from a height of 5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its kinetic energy just before it strikes the ground is:

solution.concept: Work done by gravity equals the gain in kinetic energy
solution.explanation: The only force doing work is gravity, which does work mgh on the ball as it falls through h. By the work-energy theorem this equals the gain in kinetic energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 J is the speed (10 m/s) written as an energy; 50 J halves mgh; 200 J doubles it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small stone tied to a light string 2.5 m long is whirled in a vertical circle. Taking g = 10 m/s², the least speed it must have at the highest point for the string to remain taut there is:

solution.concept: Critical speed at the top of a vertical circle
solution.explanation: At the highest point both gravity and the tension point towards the centre: T + mg = mv²/L. The string just stays taut when T = 0, so v² = gL.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5√5 m/s is √(5gL), the least speed needed at the LOWEST point; 25 m/s is gL without the square root; 5√2 m/s is √(2gL), the speed gained in falling through L, which is not the condition here.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block attached to an ideal spring is pulled slowly from the spring's natural length to an extension x and then allowed to return slowly to the natural length. The total work done by the spring force over this whole cycle is:

solution.concept: Spring force is conservative
solution.explanation: The spring force is conservative: the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions. While stretching it does −½kx², while returning it does +½kx², so the total over a closed cycle is zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: ½kx² and −½kx² are the work in only one half of the cycle; kx² adds the magnitudes of the two halves.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 1 kg, initially at rest, is acted on by a single force F = 2t along a straight line, where F is in newtons and t in seconds. The instantaneous power delivered by the force at t = 3 s is:

solution.concept: Instantaneous power P = Fv
solution.explanation: First find the velocity at t = 3 s by integrating the acceleration, then multiply by the force at that instant.
steps: At t = 3 s: F = 6 N, v = 9 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 W takes v = at = 6 × 3, treating the acceleration as constant; 27 W uses the average force 3 N; 6 W gives the force alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small block is released from rest at a height of 5 m on a smooth curved track. At the bottom the track becomes horizontal and rough, with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.5. The distance the block slides along the rough part before stopping is:

solution.concept: Work-energy theorem with gravity and friction
solution.explanation: Over the whole motion the block starts and ends at rest, so the work done by gravity (mgh) and by friction (−μmgd) add up to zero. The smooth curved part does no frictional work, and the normal force does no work.
solution.shortcut: d = h/μ; the mass and g cancel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 m equates d to h; 2.5 m multiplies h by μ instead of dividing; 20 m finds v² = 2gh = 100 m²/s² at the bottom and then forgets the 2 in d = v²/(2μg).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car of mass 800 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s along a level road. Neglecting friction and air resistance, the average power delivered to the car in these 10 s is:

solution.concept: Average power as work done divided by time
solution.explanation: The work done on the car equals its gain in kinetic energy. Average power is this work divided by the time. With uniform acceleration the instantaneous power rises steadily, so its final value is twice the average.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 kW is the instantaneous power at the end (F = 1600 N times 20 m/s); 4 kW puts the average speed 10 m/s into ½mv²; 160 kW is the work in kJ, not divided by 10 s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text:
A body moves along a straight line (the x-axis). Match List-I (feature of a graph) with List-II (the quantity it gives).

List-I:
A. Area under the force–position (F–x) graph between two positions
B. Slope of the kinetic energy–position (K–x) graph
C. Negative of the slope of the potential energy–position (U–x) graph of a conservative force
D. Slope of the kinetic energy–time (K–t) graph

List-II:
I. Power delivered by the net force
II. The conservative force at that position
III. Net force on the body along the x-axis
IV. Work done by the force between those positions

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Graphical meaning of work, force and power
solution.explanation: Work is ∫F dx, the area under F–x. By the work-energy theorem dK = F_net dx, so dK/dx = F_net and dK/dt = F_net·v, the power of the net force. For a conservative force F = −dU/dx.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the slope against position (a force) with the slope against time (a power), or the net force with the conservative force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work done by a variable force; the concept of potential energy; power
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The potential energy of a body can have a negative value.
Statement II: When only conservative forces do work on a body, its total mechanical energy remains constant, although its kinetic energy may change.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Potential energy and conservation of mechanical energy
solution.explanation: Potential energy is defined only up to an additive constant: it is measured from a chosen zero, and below that reference (for example a body below the chosen ground level, or gravitational potential energy taken zero at infinity) it is negative. So Statement I is true. With only conservative forces, K + U is constant; K and U can each change as one is converted into the other. So Statement II is true.
steps: Statement I: U depends on the reference level → can be negative → true
Statement II: conservative forces → K + U = constant, K may vary → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Only the difference of potential energy is physically fixed, not its sign; and conservation of mechanical energy does not mean that the kinetic energy stays constant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the concept of potential energy; conservation of mechanical energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 2 kg is attached to the lower end of a light vertical spring of spring constant 200 N/m whose upper end is fixed. Starting with the spring at its natural length, the block is lowered slowly by hand until it hangs at rest in equilibrium. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by the hand on the block is:

solution.concept: Work-energy theorem with gravity, spring and an applied force
solution.explanation: The block starts and ends at rest, so the total work done on it is zero. Gravity does +mgx; the spring does −½kx²; the hand, holding the block back, does the rest (negative work).
solution.shortcut: Lowered slowly to equilibrium, the spring stores only half of the gravitational PE lost; the hand takes the other half.
solution.why_others_wrong: +1 J has the wrong sign: the hand pushes up while the block moves down; −2 J ignores the spring; zero assumes gravity and the spring do equal and opposite work.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring; the work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wooden block of mass 0.95 kg hangs at rest from a light inextensible string 0.4 m long. A bullet of mass 50 g moving horizontally strikes the block and gets embedded in it. Taking g = 10 m/s², the least speed of the bullet for which the block (with the bullet) just completes a vertical circle is:

solution.concept: Momentum conservation in the impact, then energy conservation in the vertical circle
solution.explanation: During the brief impact, momentum is conserved (kinetic energy is not). Just after the impact the block must have at least √(5gL) at the lowest point to go round the circle on a string.
steps: Needed speed of block after impact: V = √(5gL) = √20 = 2√5 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 40√2 m/s uses √(2gL), which only raises the block to the level of the support; 40 m/s uses √(4gL), the condition for a light rod; 2√5 m/s is the block's speed, not the bullet's.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle; collisions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The tension in the string of a swinging simple pendulum does no work on the bob.
Reason (R): The tension in the string of a swinging simple pendulum has the same magnitude at every point of the swing.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Work done by a force perpendicular to the displacement
solution.explanation: The bob moves along an arc of a circle centred on the point of support, so its displacement at every instant is along the tangent, perpendicular to the string. The tension is along the string, so T·dr = 0 and the tension does no work: A is true. The tension is not constant: it must supply mv²/L plus the radial component of weight, T = mg cos θ + mv²/L, which is largest at the lowest point. So R is false.
steps: R: T = mg cos θ + mv²/L varies with θ and v → false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so options A and B are wrong; A is true, so D is wrong. The work is zero because of the direction of the tension, whatever its magnitude.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the scalar product and work
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A block of mass 1 kg moving at 2 m/s on a smooth horizontal surface strikes the free end of a light horizontal spring of spring constant 100 N/m, whose other end is fixed to a wall. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The greatest force exerted by the spring on the block is 20 N.
(b) When the compression is 0.1 m, the speed of the block is √3 m/s.
(c) While the spring is being compressed, the spring force does +2 J of work on the block.
(d) The block leaves the spring with a speed of 2 m/s, moving away from the wall.
(e) Over the whole interaction, the net work done by the spring force on the block is +2 J.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Conservation of energy with an ideal spring
solution.explanation: All the kinetic energy (2 J) is stored at maximum compression, ½kx_m² = 2 J, so x_m = 0.2 m. The spring force opposes the block while it compresses (negative work) and pushes it back while it extends (positive work).
steps: (c) compression: W = −2 J, not +2 J → false
(d) energy conserved → leaves at 2 m/s, reversed, true
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) has the wrong sign; (e) forgets that the block leaves with the same speed it came in with, so the net work is zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A constant torque of 5 N m acts on a wheel about its fixed axle while the wheel turns through 4 complete revolutions. The work done by the torque is:

solution.concept: Work done by a torque
solution.explanation: For rotation about a fixed axis, the work done by a constant torque is W = τθ, with θ in radians, just as W = Fs in linear motion.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 J multiplies the torque by the number of revolutions; 20π J uses π rad per revolution; 40 J uses 2 rad per revolution, dropping π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', work done by a torque

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The engine of a machine applies a constant torque of 20 N m to a shaft rotating steadily at 10 rad/s about its axis. The power delivered to the shaft is:

solution.concept: Power in rotational motion
solution.explanation: Instantaneous power in rotation is P = τω, the analogue of P = Fv.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 W divides the torque by ω; 20 W ignores ω; 100 W takes half the product, confusing P with a kinetic energy expression.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', power in rotational motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: The moment of inertia of a body of mass 2 kg about a certain axis is 0.18 kg m². Its radius of gyration about this axis is:

solution.concept: Radius of gyration
solution.explanation: The radius of gyration k about an axis is defined by I = Mk²: it is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass, placed as a point, would have the same moment of inertia.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.09 m forgets the square root; 0.36 m multiplies I by M; 0.6 m doubles the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia (radius of gyration)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The SI unit of angular momentum can also be written as:

solution.concept: Units of angular momentum
solution.explanation: Angular momentum L = r × p has unit m × kg m s⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻¹. Since 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻², this is the same as J s (also the unit of Planck's constant).
steps: J s = kg m² s⁻² × s = kg m² s⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: N m (= kg m² s⁻²) is the unit of torque; kg m² s⁻² is the same unit written in base units; W s is the joule, a unit of energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular momentum of a particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A thin spherical shell has mass 3 kg and radius 0.2 m. Its moment of inertia about a diameter is (2/3)MR². Its moment of inertia about a tangent to its surface is:

solution.concept: Theorem of parallel axes
solution.explanation: A tangent is parallel to a diameter at a distance R from it. By the parallel axis theorem, I = I_cm + MR² = (2/3 + 1)MR² = (5/3)MR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.08 kg m² is the moment of inertia about a diameter; 0.168 kg m² uses (7/5)MR², the result for a SOLID sphere; 0.12 kg m² is MR² alone, leaving out I_cm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', theorem of parallel axes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin rod 3 m long lies along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 3 m. Its mass per unit length increases with x as λ = kx, where k is a constant. The position of its centre of mass is:

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a continuous body
solution.explanation: For a continuous body, X = ∫x dm / ∫dm with dm = λ dx. Because the rod is heavier towards x = 3 m, the centre of mass lies beyond the midpoint.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 m treats the rod as uniform; 1 m is L/3, measured from the wrong end; 2.25 m uses ∫x³/∫x² (as if λ ∝ x²).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass of a continuous body

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A thin uniform straight wire of mass M and length L has moment of inertia I₁ about an axis perpendicular to it through its midpoint. The same wire is bent into a circular ring, whose moment of inertia about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane is I₂. The ratio I₂/I₁ is:

solution.concept: Moment of inertia of a rod and a ring
solution.explanation: For the straight wire I₁ = ML²/12. Bent into a ring, the circumference is L, so R = L/(2π) and I₂ = MR² = ML²/(4π²).
solution.why_others_wrong: π²/3 is the inverse ratio; 12/π² takes R = L/π (forgetting the 2 in 2πR); 3/(2π²) uses MR²/2, the moment of inertia of a ring about a diameter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moments of inertia of some regular shaped bodies

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A particle of mass 1 kg is at the point r = 2î m. Match List-I (its velocity, in m/s) with List-II (its angular momentum about the origin, in kg m² s⁻¹).

List-I:
A. v = 3ĵ
B. v = 3î
C. v = −3ĵ
D. v = 3k̂

List-II:
I. Zero
II. −6ĵ
III. 6k̂
IV. −6k̂

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Angular momentum as a vector product, l = r × p
solution.explanation: l = r × p = m(r × v). Use î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × î = −k̂, î × î = 0 and î × k̂ = −ĵ.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes reverse the sign for v = ±3ĵ, take î × k̂ = +ĵ, or give a non-zero angular momentum when the velocity is along r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular momentum of a particle
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If no external torque acts on a body rotating about a fixed axis, its angular velocity must remain constant.
Statement II: The kinetic energy of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity ω is ½Iω², where I is its moment of inertia about that axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum versus constant angular velocity
solution.explanation: With no external torque the angular momentum Iω is conserved, not ω itself. If the body changes shape and its moment of inertia changes (a skater pulling in her arms, a diver tucking), ω changes. So Statement I is false. Statement II is the standard result K = Σ½mᵢ(rᵢω)² = ½Iω², true.
steps: Statement I: τ = 0 → Iω constant; I can change → ω can change → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I would hold only for a body whose moment of inertia cannot change, such as a rigid wheel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum; kinematics of rotational motion
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A thin uniform square plate has mass M and side a. Its moment of inertia about an axis in its plane, passing through its centre and parallel to one side, is Ma²/12. Its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plate and passing through one corner is:

solution.concept: Perpendicular and parallel axes theorems together
solution.explanation: First use the perpendicular axes theorem at the centre: the axis perpendicular to the plate through the centre has I = Ma²/12 + Ma²/12 = Ma²/6. Then shift it parallel to the corner, a distance a/√2 away.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ma²/3 is the moment of inertia about a side (in the plane); 7Ma²/12 starts from Ma²/12 instead of using the perpendicular axes theorem; 7Ma²/6 takes the shift distance as a instead of a/√2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', theorems of perpendicular and parallel axes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Treat the Earth as a uniform solid sphere spinning about its axis once in 24 h. Suppose it contracted, with no external torque and no change of mass, until its radius was half its present value. The new length of the day and the factor by which its rotational kinetic energy would change are:

options.text: 12 h; rotational kinetic energy becomes 2 times
6 h; rotational kinetic energy is unchanged
6 h; rotational kinetic energy becomes 4 times
96 h; rotational kinetic energy becomes 1/4 times

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum and the energy that goes with it
solution.explanation: With no external torque, L = Iω is constant. For a uniform sphere I = (2/5)MR², so halving R makes I one quarter, and ω four times as large. Rotational KE = L²/(2I), so with L fixed it rises four times; the extra energy comes from the work done by the internal forces during contraction.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 h and 2 times assume I ∝ R instead of R²; 'unchanged' wrongly assumes rotational KE is conserved along with L; 96 h inverts the change in ω.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum
solution.final_answer: Option C: 6 h; rotational kinetic energy becomes 4 times

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A rigid body cannot be in rotational equilibrium while a non-zero net external force acts on it.
Reason (R): Translational equilibrium requires the net external force to be zero and rotational equilibrium requires the net external torque to be zero; the two conditions are independent of each other.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conditions of translational and rotational equilibrium
solution.explanation: R is true: the two conditions of mechanical equilibrium are separate. A body can satisfy one without the other. For example, a single force acting through the centre of mass of a free body accelerates it but gives zero torque about the centre of mass, so the body is in rotational equilibrium while the net force is not zero. So A is false.
steps: R: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 are independent conditions → true
A: net force ≠ 0 with net torque = 0 is possible → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Because A is false, options A, B and C are wrong. A couple shows the converse: zero net force with a non-zero torque.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
On a smooth horizontal surface, a particle of mass 2 kg is at x = 0 moving at 3 m/s in the +x direction and, at the same instant, a particle of mass 1 kg is at x = 6 m moving at 3 m/s in the −x direction. They move along the x-axis, collide and stick together. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At the initial instant the centre of mass of the two particles is at x = 2 m.
(b) The velocity of the centre of mass is 2 m/s in the +x direction.
(c) After the collision the combined body moves at 1 m/s in the +x direction.
(d) The particles collide at x = 3 m, which is also where the centre of mass is at that instant.
(e) The total kinetic energy of the particles is the same after the collision as before it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Motion of the centre of mass of an isolated system
solution.explanation: No external horizontal force acts, so the centre of mass moves with a constant velocity, before and after the collision. The combined body after sticking moves with the velocity of the centre of mass.
steps: (c) the stuck pair moves with V = 1 m/s, true
(d) closing speed 6 m/s, gap 6 m → t = 1 s; x = 3 m; X(1 s) = 2 + 1 = 3 m, true
(e) K before = 9 + 4.5 = 13.5 J, after = ½ × 3 × 1² = 1.5 J → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) adds speeds without the signs of the velocities; (e) ignores that a sticking (perfectly inelastic) collision always loses kinetic energy, here 12 J.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass; linear momentum of a system of particles

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking the Earth's radius as 6400 km and g = 10 m/s² at its surface, and neglecting air resistance and the Earth's rotation, the minimum energy that must be given to a body of mass 1000 kg at the Earth's surface so that it escapes from the Earth's gravity is:

solution.concept: Energy needed for escape
solution.explanation: With the zero of potential energy at infinity, the body at the surface has U = −GMm/R. To escape it needs at least enough kinetic energy to bring its total energy to zero: K = GMm/R = mgR, since GM = gR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.2 × 10¹⁰ J is mgR/2, the energy to raise the body only to a height R; 1.28 × 10¹¹ J doubles mgR; 6.4 × 10⁷ J uses R in kilometres.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', escape speed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and the gravitational potential to be zero at infinity, the gravitational potential at a distance of 3 m from a point mass of 45 kg is about:

solution.concept: Gravitational potential of a point mass
solution.explanation: The gravitational potential at distance r from a point mass M is V = −GM/r: the work done per unit mass by an external agent in bringing a test mass slowly from infinity. It is negative because gravity is attractive.
solution.why_others_wrong: −3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ divides by r² (that is the field strength, in N kg⁻¹); +1.0 × 10⁻⁹ has the wrong sign; −3.0 × 10⁻⁹ forgets to divide by r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy (gravitational potential)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (scientist) with List-II (contribution described in NCERT's account of gravitation).

List-I:
A. Ptolemy
B. Tycho Brahe
C. Johannes Kepler
D. Galileo Galilei

List-II:
I. Recognised that all bodies, irrespective of their masses, are accelerated towards the Earth with a constant acceleration
II. Proposed a geocentric model in which the planets move round the Earth
III. Made detailed observations of the positions of the planets with the naked eye
IV. Analysed these observations and arrived at three laws of planetary motion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: History of the study of gravitation
solution.explanation: NCERT's introduction to gravitation: Ptolemy's geocentric model; Tycho Brahe's naked-eye observations of planetary positions; Kepler's three laws drawn from Brahe's data; Galileo's finding that all bodies fall with the same constant acceleration.
steps: Kepler → three laws of planetary motion (IV)
Galileo → equal acceleration of falling bodies (I)
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes exchange the observer (Brahe) with the analyst (Kepler), or give Galileo's result on falling bodies to Kepler.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', introduction and Kepler's laws
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two identical uniform solid spheres of the same material are placed in contact. If each sphere is replaced by one of the same material but twice the radius, again placed in contact, the gravitational force between them becomes:

solution.concept: Scaling of the gravitational force with size
solution.explanation: For a uniform sphere M = (4/3)πR³ρ, so doubling R makes each mass 8 times. The distance between the centres of touching spheres is 2R, so it doubles. Each sphere attracts as a point mass at its centre.
steps: F = GM²/(2R)² with M ∝ R³ → F ∝ R⁶/R² = R⁴
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 times treats the mass as proportional to R; 64 times ignores the larger separation; 1/4 times keeps the masses fixed and only doubles the separation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin uniform ring has mass M and radius R. Taking the gravitational potential to be zero at infinity, the minimum work needed to move a particle of mass m slowly from the centre of the ring to a point on its axis at a distance √3R from the centre is (G is the universal gravitational constant):

solution.concept: Gravitational potential by superposition
solution.explanation: Potential is a scalar, so add the contributions −G dM/s of all mass elements. Every element of the ring is the same distance s from a point on the axis: s = R at the centre and s = √(R² + 3R²) = 2R at the second point. The work done by an external agent is m(V_final − V_initial).
solution.why_others_wrong: −GMm/(2R) has the sign reversed (the agent must do positive work to pull m away from the ring); GMm/R assumes the far point is at zero potential; (GMm/R)(1 − 1/√3) takes the distance from the ring as √3R instead of 2R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a height h much smaller than the Earth's radius R, the gain in gravitational potential energy when a body of mass m is raised from the surface to the height h may be taken as mgh.
Reason (R): The exact gain is GMm/R − GMm/(R + h) = GMmh/[R(R + h)], which is nearly GMmh/R² = mgh when h ≪ R.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: mgh as an approximation to −GMm/r
solution.explanation: The general expression for gravitational potential energy is −GMm/r. The difference between r = R + h and r = R reduces to GMmh/R² when R + h ≈ R, and GM/R² = g. So R is exactly the derivation of A.
steps: Both true; R explains A → option A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the reason, not a separate fact, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If the mass of the Earth were doubled with its radius unchanged, the escape speed from its surface would become √2 times its present value.
Statement II: If both the mass and the radius of the Earth were doubled, the acceleration due to gravity at its surface would remain unchanged.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Dependence of escape speed and g on mass and radius
solution.explanation: v_e = √(2GM/R): doubling M alone multiplies it by √2, so Statement I is true. g = GM/R²: doubling both M and R gives 2/4 = 1/2, so g would halve, and Statement II is false. (It is the escape speed, ∝ √(M/R), that would stay unchanged.)
steps: Statement I: v_e ∝ √M at fixed R → √2 times → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II applies the M/R ratio, which governs escape speed, to g, which depends on M/R².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity of the earth; escape speed
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two stars of masses M and 2M, a distance d apart, revolve in circles about their common centre of mass under their mutual gravitational attraction alone. Their common period of revolution is (G is the universal gravitational constant):

solution.concept: Gravitation with the centre of mass: a binary system
solution.explanation: Each star moves on a circle about the centre of mass, not about the other star. The star of mass M is at 2d/3 from the centre of mass. The gravitational force between the stars, G(M)(2M)/d², supplies its centripetal force Mω²(2d/3).
solution.shortcut: For two bodies, ω² = G(m₁ + m₂)/d³: here G(3M)/d³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2π√(d³/(GM)) treats the star M as orbiting a fixed mass M at distance d; 2π√(d³/(2GM)) has M orbit the fixed 2M star at distance d; 2π√(d³/(4GM)) takes the centre of mass at the midpoint d/2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation; 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body at rest on the Earth's surface needs a minimum energy E₁ to be thrown vertically up to a height equal to the Earth's radius R, and a minimum energy E₂ to be placed in a circular orbit at a height R above the surface. Neglecting air resistance and the Earth's rotation, E₁ : E₂ is:

solution.concept: Energy of a body at a height versus energy of a satellite
solution.explanation: To just reach height R the body only needs the rise in potential energy. To orbit at radius 2R it must also have the orbital kinetic energy GMm/(2·2R); its total energy there is −GMm/(4R).
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 2 inverts the ratio; 1 : 1 forgets the satellite's kinetic energy; 1 : 2 adds the kinetic energy of an orbit at the SURFACE, GMm/(2R), instead of at radius 2R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', energy of an orbiting satellite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A satellite in a circular orbit of radius 2r round the Earth is shifted to a circular orbit of radius r. Taking the potential energy to be zero at infinity, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its kinetic energy becomes twice as large.
(b) Its gravitational potential energy increases.
(c) Its total mechanical energy decreases.
(d) Its orbital speed becomes √2 times as large.
(e) Its period of revolution becomes half as large.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dependence of satellite energies, speed and period on orbit radius
solution.explanation: K = GMm/(2r), U = −GMm/r and E = −GMm/(2r); v = √(GM/r) and T ∝ r^(3/2). Halving the radius doubles K, doubles the magnitude of both U and E (making them more negative), raises v by √2 and reduces T by a factor 2√2.
steps: (b) U = −GMm/r becomes more negative → it decreases → false
(c) E = −GMm/(2r) becomes more negative → decreases, true
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) confuses a larger magnitude with a larger value: −2x is less than −x. (e) uses T ∝ r instead of Kepler's T² ∝ r³.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites; energy of an orbiting satellite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The coefficient of viscosity of a liquid is 0.5 poise, where 1 poise = 1 g cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ (the CGS unit). Its value in SI units is:

solution.concept: Conversion between CGS and SI units of viscosity
solution.explanation: 1 g cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 10⁻³ kg / (10⁻² m × 1 s) = 0.1 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 0.1 Pa s. So 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s.
steps: 1 poise = 10⁻³ kg × 10² m⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 0.1 Pa s
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 Pa s multiplies by 10 instead of dividing; 0.5 Pa s assumes the two units are equal; 0.005 Pa s divides by 100 instead of 10, treating 1 poise as 10⁻² Pa s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', viscosity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water flows out of a small hole in the side of a wide open tank, 5 m below the free surface of the water. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed of efflux is:

solution.concept: Torricelli's law
solution.explanation: Applying Bernoulli's principle between the free surface (speed ≈ 0, pressure Pₐ) and the hole (pressure Pₐ), the speed of efflux is √(2gh), the speed a body gains in falling freely through h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 m/s forgets the square root; 5√2 m/s uses √(gh); 50 m/s uses gh.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Bernoulli's principle (speed of efflux: Torricelli's law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On a new temperature scale X, the melting point of ice is 20 °X and the boiling point of water is 220 °X, both at standard pressure, and the scale is linear. A temperature of 50 °C on this scale is:

solution.concept: Relation between linear temperature scales
solution.explanation: For any two linear scales, (reading − ice point)/(steam point − ice point) is the same. So (X − 20)/(220 − 20) = (C − 0)/(100 − 0).
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 °X forgets to add the ice-point offset of 20; 70 °X just adds 20 to 50; 110 °X multiplies 50 by 220/100 without the offset.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', temperature and heat; measurement of temperature

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Cooking pots are often given a copper coating on the bottom mainly because copper:

options.text: Is a poor conductor of heat, so it keeps the heat inside the food
Is a good conductor of heat, so it spreads the heat over the bottom of the pot
Has a very high specific heat capacity, so it stores a large amount of heat
Reflects heat radiation back into the pot

solution.concept: Thermal conductivity and its uses
solution.explanation: Copper has a high thermal conductivity. A copper-coated bottom conducts heat quickly and spreads it evenly over the base, so the food is heated uniformly.
steps: Good conductor → faster, more uniform heating of the pot's base
solution.why_others_wrong: Copper is a good, not a poor, conductor; its specific heat capacity is low, not high; reflection of radiation is not why it is used on the bottom of a pot heated by a flame.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', heat transfer (conduction)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Is a good conductor of heat, so it spreads the heat over the bottom of the pot

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The ropes of cranes used to lift heavy loads are made of a large number of thin wires braided together, rather than of a single thick wire of the same total cross-section. The main reason is that the braided rope:

options.text: Is easier to manufacture and more flexible, while giving the required strength
Has a much larger Young's modulus than a single wire of the same material
Is lighter for the same cross-sectional area of metal
Stretches more under the load, so it stores more energy

solution.concept: Application of elastic behaviour: design of crane ropes
solution.explanation: The required radius of the rope is fixed by the load and the yield strength of steel (with a safety factor). A single thick wire of that radius would be practically a rigid rod; braiding many thin wires gives the same strength with ease of manufacture, flexibility and strength.
steps: Required cross-section is set by load and yield strength
Many thin braided wires → flexible, easy to make
solution.why_others_wrong: Young's modulus is a property of the material, not of how the wires are arranged; the mass of metal for the same cross-section is the same; extra stretching is not the aim.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', applications of elastic behaviour of materials
solution.final_answer: Option A: Is easier to manufacture and more flexible, while giving the required strength

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A sphere radiates energy at the rate P as a black body at absolute temperature T. Another black-body sphere has twice the radius and is at an absolute temperature T/2. The rate at which it radiates energy is:

solution.concept: Stefan-Boltzmann law
solution.explanation: The power radiated by a black body is P = σAT⁴, with A = 4πr² for a sphere. So P ∝ r²T⁴.
solution.why_others_wrong: P/2 uses T² instead of T⁴; 4P ignores the change in temperature; P/8 takes the area as proportional to r instead of r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An air bubble of radius 0.1 mm is formed 10 cm below the surface of water in an open vessel. The surface tension of water is 0.07 N/m, its density is 1000 kg/m³, the atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 10 m/s². The pressure inside the bubble is:

solution.concept: Pressure inside an air bubble in a liquid
solution.explanation: The water just outside the bubble is at Pₐ + ρgh. An air bubble in a liquid has one liquid surface, so the pressure inside exceeds this by 2S/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.014 × 10⁵ Pa leaves out the hydrostatic pressure ρgh; 1.010 × 10⁵ Pa leaves out the surface-tension term; 1.038 × 10⁵ Pa uses 4S/r, which applies to a soap bubble with two surfaces.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface tension (excess pressure inside a drop and a bubble)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The coefficient of volume expansion of a liquid is 5 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. When the liquid is heated through 40 K, its density decreases by about:

solution.concept: Change of density with temperature
solution.explanation: The mass stays fixed while the volume grows by the factor (1 + γΔT), so ρ' = ρ/(1 + γΔT) ≈ ρ(1 − γΔT) when γΔT ≪ 1. The fractional decrease in density is γΔT.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.67% treats 5 × 10⁻⁴ as a volume coefficient and divides by 3; 6% multiplies by 3, treating the given value as a linear coefficient; 0.02% leaves out the factor 100.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The walls of an ice box have a total area of 1.0 m² and a thickness of 5 cm, and are made of a material of thermal conductivity 0.021 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. The ice box contains ice at 0 °C and the outside temperature is 40 °C. Taking the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ and neglecting heat flow other than by conduction through the walls, the mass of ice that melts in one hour is:

solution.concept: Steady-state conduction combined with latent heat
solution.explanation: In the steady state the heat current through the walls is H = KAΔT/d. All this heat melts ice at 0 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 g is the mass melted in one minute; 1.8 g puts the thickness as 5 m instead of 0.05 m (a factor 100); 0.18 g leaves the answer in the wrong unit (0.18 kg read as grams).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', conduction; latent heat

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, that of ice as 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ and the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Match List-I (process, at standard pressure) with List-II (heat needed).

List-I:
A. Warming 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 30 °C
B. Melting 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C
C. Turning 0.1 kg of water at 100 °C into steam at 100 °C
D. Warming 1 kg of ice from −10 °C to 0 °C (without melting it)

List-II:
I. 226 kJ
II. 21 kJ
III. 42 kJ
IV. 336 kJ

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Sensible heat (mcΔT) and latent heat (mL)
solution.explanation: A change of temperature needs Q = mcΔT; a change of state at constant temperature needs Q = mL.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the specific heats of ice and water, or the two latent heats (forgetting that only 0.1 kg is vaporised).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', specific heat capacity; change of state (latent heat)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Within the elastic limit, the elastic potential energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire is ½ × stress × strain.
Statement II: For the same tensile stress, a wire of a material with a larger Young's modulus stores more elastic energy per unit volume.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Elastic potential energy density
solution.explanation: The work done in stretching a wire is ½Fl, so the energy per unit volume is ½(F/A)(l/L) = ½ × stress × strain: Statement I is true.
